subject: chemistry
question_text: Calculate the oxidation number of the chromium atom in Cr₂O₇²⁻.

verification.note: Chapter 5 (Stoichiometry) is sourced from the Sri Chaitanya Junior Fastrack chemistry section (book pp.66-72), which prints the question, its star rank and a model answer. Only ONE source book is held for chemistry — the TSBIE Basic Learning Material in hand covers physics only — so the two-book union check is PENDING a second chemistry source. This chapter has NO Long Answer section in the book, so no 8-mark form is invented. The 1+1 mark split is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it; the question itself is sourced, not invented.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Rules and the equation
lines: Rules applied: O = −2, and the oxidation
numbers in an ION add up to the charge
Let the oxidation number of Cr be x.
steps.why: Cr₂O₇²⁻ is an ion, not a neutral compound, so the sum of oxidation numbers must equal its charge −2, not zero. That single change is the point of this question.
common_mistakes: Setting the sum equal to 0. For an ion the sum equals the ion's charge, −2 here.
Forgetting the factor 2 on x for the two chromium atoms.
steps.memory_tip: Neutral compound: sum = 0. Ion: sum = the charge written at its top right.
steps.margin_note: The equation set equal to −2 (not 0) earns this mark.

steps.label: The answer

lines.text: x = +6, so the oxidation number of Cr in Cr₂O₇²⁻ is +6

steps.why: Moving −14 across gives 2x = 12, and halving it gives +6 for each chromium atom.
common_mistakes: Stopping at 2x = +12 and reporting +12. The question asks for ONE chromium atom.
Sign slip when moving −14 across, giving 2x = −16.
steps.memory_tip: Chromium is +6 in dichromate and chromate both — the same x answers two common questions.
steps.margin_note: Box +6 for one Cr atom, not +12 for the pair.

insider_note: The examiner checks the right-hand side of the very first equation: −2 for the ion's charge is the whole question, and 0 there loses the set-up mark.
